title: Chapter 2: The Macroeconomic Production Possibilities Frontier & Capital Deepening
benchmark: Paul Krugman & Robin Wells, Macroeconomics (Principles SSOT, Spring 2027)

questions.title: Distinguishing Consumer Goods from Capital Goods
questions.prompt_template: In the macroeconomic Production Possibilities Frontier (PPF), what fundamentally distinguishes Capital Goods (I) from Consumer Goods (C)?

hints.text: Think about how each category affects household satisfaction today versus productive capacity in future years.
Capital goods include equipment, factories, and power-grid assets, whereas consumer goods include groceries and restaurant meals.

options_template.text: Capital goods are durable assets produced today to expand future output, whereas consumer goods provide immediate household satisfaction without expanding future productive capacity.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Capital goods (such as semiconductor fabs, servers, and transformers) raise workers' future productive capacity, whereas consumer goods satisfy current wants and are used up.

options_template.text: Capital goods are always produced by the government, whereas consumer goods are exclusively produced by private firms.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Public-Private Confusion): Both private firms and governments produce capital goods (such as private factories or public ports); the distinction rests on durable productive use, not ownership.

options_template.text: Capital goods consist of corporate stocks and government bonds, whereas consumer goods consist of physical retail merchandise.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Financial vs. Economic Investment): In macroeconomics, capital goods are physical machinery, structures, and software—not financial securities like stocks or bonds.

options_template.text: Capital goods are consumed within a single year, whereas consumer goods permanently increase a nation's labor force.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Role Reversal): Consumer goods are used up for immediate satisfaction, while durable capital goods last across years to expand future productive capacity.

questions.title: Economic Investment vs. Financial Asset Purchases
questions.prompt_template: Which of the following transactions counts as macroeconomic investment (I) on the macroeconomic Production Possibilities Frontier?

hints.text: Recall the distinction between creating new physical productive capacity and transferring ownership of paper assets.
Macroeconomic investment (I) requires newly produced physical machinery, buildings, or software.

options_template.text: A household purchasing $50,000 of shares in a publicly traded semiconductor company on the stock exchange.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Financial vs. Economic Investment): Buying existing stock merely transfers ownership of a financial claim; it does not produce new physical capital.

options_template.text: A logistics firm constructing a new automated warehouse and installing robotic sorting equipment.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Building new structures and installing machinery adds newly produced physical capital goods that expand future productive capacity.

options_template.text: A pension fund buying $10 million of previously issued U.S. Treasury bonds.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Financial vs. Economic Investment): Purchasing existing bonds is financial saving/portfolio allocation, not physical capital production.

options_template.text: An investor exchanging U.S. dollars for cryptocurrency on a digital trading platform.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Financial vs. Economic Investment): Trading digital financial assets does not create durable factories, tools, or software that expand real national output.

questions.title: Meaning of the Macroeconomic Intertemporal Trade-Off
questions.prompt_template: Why does selecting a point on the macroeconomic Production Possibilities Frontier create an intertemporal trade-off?

hints.text: Break down the word 'intertemporal'—it refers to a trade-off across time.
Finite resources in the current year must be split between enjoying output now (C) and building tools for later (I).

options_template.text: Because total annual resources are scarce, devoting more output to current consumption leaves fewer resources for capital goods that expand future living standards.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Shifting engineers, steel, electricity, and construction crews toward consumer goods raises satisfaction today at the cost of slower future frontier expansion.

options_template.text: Because increasing capital goods production today permanently reduces the size of the labor force in future decades.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (False Labor-Capital Trade-Off): Producing capital goods reallocates current resources away from current consumption, not away from future population or labor supply.

options_template.text: Because countries must choose between trading with foreign partners today or producing domestically tomorrow.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Trade vs. Intertemporal Choice): An intertemporal trade-off is between present consumption and future productive capacity, not between international trade and autarky.

options_template.text: Because any increase in current consumption automatically destroys existing factories through hyperinflation.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inflation Conflation): High consumption limits new capital formation relative to depreciation, rather than directly destroying factories through hyperinflation.

questions.title: Positive Gross Investment with Shrinking Capital Stock
questions.prompt_template: Under what condition can an economy record positive gross investment (I > 0) during a year while its total physical capital stock actually shrinks?

hints.text: Write down the net investment identity connecting gross investment (I) and depreciation (delta * K).
The capital stock shrinks whenever net investment (Delta K = I - delta * K) is negative.

options_template.text: Whenever gross investment exceeds annual depreciation (I > delta * K).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Reversal): When gross investment exceeds depreciation, net investment is positive and the capital stock expands.

options_template.text: Whenever consumer goods output is larger than capital goods output (C > I).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (C vs. I Comparison Error): Most growing economies produce far more consumer goods than capital goods; capital stock growth depends on comparing I to depreciation, not to C.

options_template.text: Whenever gross investment is positive but smaller than annual physical depreciation (0 < I < delta * K).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because net investment is Delta K = I - delta * K, if newly built capital does not replace worn-out or obsolete equipment, Delta K is negative and the capital stock contracts.

options_template.text: Whenever gross investment exactly equals annual depreciation (I = delta * K).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Stationary vs. Contracting Stock): When I = delta * K, net investment is zero and the capital stock remains constant rather than shrinking.

questions.title: Why the Zero-Consumption Trap Is Infeasible
questions.prompt_template: Why can a real-world economy never sustain a strategy of investing 100% of its GDP in capital goods (C = 0) to maximize future growth?

hints.text: Consider what households and workers physically require in order to survive and operate machinery.
Without minimum consumption of food, housing, and healthcare, the labor force cannot function.

options_template.text: Because international accounting rules prohibit countries from investing more than 10% of GDP.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Institutional Myth): No international accounting rule caps investment at 10% of GDP; the constraint is biological and economic.

options_template.text: Because zero consumption immediately eliminates all physical depreciation on existing machinery.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Depreciation Misconception): Depreciation occurs from wear, tear, and obsolescence regardless of whether consumption falls to zero.

options_template.text: Because financial markets require consumer spending to issue corporate stocks.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Financial Market Confusion): The fundamental barrier to C = 0 is physical survival of workers, not stock market issuance rules.

options_template.text: Because workers require food, housing, and healthcare (consumer goods) to survive and operate the capital stock.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The Zero-Consumption Trap highlights that some minimum level of consumption is essential to sustain the workforce needed to build and run capital goods.

questions.title: Defining Potential GDP (Y*)
questions.prompt_template: How do macroeconomists define Potential GDP (Y*) in relation to the macroeconomic Production Possibilities Frontier?

hints.text: Think about whether Potential GDP represents an absolute physical ceiling or a sustainable full-employment benchmark.
Remember that factories can temporarily run overtime beyond normal capacity, creating inflationary pressure.

options_template.text: The absolute physical maximum output possible if every citizen worked 24 hours a day with zero machine maintenance.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Hard Physical Ceiling Fallacy): Potential GDP is not a hard physical wall; it measures normal sustainable full-employment output, which can be briefly exceeded during overheating.

options_template.text: The maximum sustainable level of real output an economy can produce when its labor force, factories, and technology operate at normal full-employment utilization.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Operating on the PPF corresponds to actual real GDP equaling Potential GDP (Y = Y*), reflecting sustainable full-employment resource use.

options_template.text: The average nominal GDP recorded during the most recent recessionary downturn.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Recessionary Baseline Confusion): Recessionary output lies below Potential GDP (Y < Y*), and Potential GDP is measured in real, not nominal, terms.

options_template.text: The total market value of all financial assets and government debt held by domestic households.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Stock vs. Flow / Financial Confusion): Potential GDP is a flow of real goods and services produced per year, not a stock of financial wealth.

questions.title: Economic Meaning of a Recessionary Output Gap
questions.prompt_template: When an economy experiences a recessionary output gap (Y < Y*), what has happened to its productive resources?

hints.text: Distinguish between resources being physically destroyed versus sitting temporarily idle.
Ask whether a typical business-cycle downturn erases the PPF or moves the economy inside it.

options_template.text: Existing factories, machinery, and skilled workers still exist, but weak aggregate spending leaves them temporarily idle inside the PPF.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A recessionary output gap reflects underutilization of existing resources (Y < Y*), placing the economy at an inefficient interior point without destroying the physical frontier.

options_template.text: The nation's physical capital stock and technological knowledge have permanently vanished, collapsing the PPF inward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cyclical vs. Structural Confusion): Standard recessions reflect idle capacity inside an intact PPF rather than permanent physical destruction of capital or technology.

options_template.text: Workers are running unsustainable overtime shifts that push output temporarily above normal capacity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Overheating Reversal): Unsustainable overtime describes overheating (Y > Y*), the exact opposite of a recessionary gap (Y < Y*).

options_template.text: The economy has achieved full employment and can only expand output by inventing new technology.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Full-Employment Assumption): Inside the PPF, output can expand through cyclical recovery by rehiring idle workers without needing new technology first.

questions.title: Characteristics of Macroeconomic Overheating
questions.prompt_template: What does it mean when actual real GDP temporarily exceeds Potential GDP (Y > Y*)?

hints.text: Recall that Potential GDP is normal sustainable capacity, not an unbreakable physical wall.
Consider what happens to overtime shifts, supply chains, and inflation when demand surges past normal capacity.

options_template.text: The economy has permanently shifted its long-run PPF outward through a sudden surge in Total Factor Productivity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Temporary vs. Permanent Capacity): Overheating (Y > Y*) is a temporary demand-driven stretch beyond normal capacity, not a permanent shift in Y*.

options_template.text: The economy is operating inside its PPF with high cyclical unemployment and falling prices.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Recessionary Gap Confusion): High cyclical unemployment and operating inside the PPF describe a recessionary gap (Y < Y*), not overheating.

options_template.text: Aggregate demand is temporarily pushing factories into unsustainable overtime and straining capacity, generating inflationary bottlenecks.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because Y* reflects normal sustainable utilization, a short-lived demand surge can push Y > Y* through overtime and strained supply chains, fueling inflation.

options_template.text: Net investment has become negative because depreciation exceeds gross capital formation.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Depreciation Conflation): Overheating is a short-run demand phenomenon relative to Y*, whereas negative net investment is a capital-accounting condition.

questions.title: Contrasting Cyclical Recovery and Secular Growth
questions.prompt_template: Which statement accurately contrasts short-run cyclical recovery with long-run secular economic growth?

hints.text: Compare closing an existing gap (Y approaching Y*) with expanding capacity itself (Y*_1 rising to Y*_2).
Think about the roles of rehiring idle inputs versus expanding K, human capital, and Total Factor Productivity (A).

options_template.text: Cyclical recovery shifts the PPF outward permanently, whereas secular growth merely eliminates temporary unemployment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Term Reversal): This swaps the two definitions—secular growth shifts the PPF outward, while cyclical recovery eliminates idle capacity.

options_template.text: Both cyclical recovery and secular growth are caused exclusively by cutting interest rates and mailing stimulus checks.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Only Growth Fallacy): Demand stimulus helps close recessionary gaps, but long-run secular growth requires supply-side capital deepening, human capital, and TFP.

options_template.text: Cyclical recovery requires increasing Total Factor Productivity (A), whereas secular growth only requires reopening shuttered factories.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cause Reversal): Reopening shuttered factories is cyclical recovery, whereas raising Total Factor Productivity drives secular growth.

options_template.text: Cyclical recovery moves the economy from an interior point back onto its existing PPF, whereas secular growth shifts the entire PPF and Potential GDP outward.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Recovery puts idle labor and machinery back to work (Y -> Y*_1), while secular growth expands productive capacity itself (Y*_1 -> Y*_2).

questions.title: Defining Capital Deepening (k = K/L)
questions.prompt_template: What is the precise economic definition of capital deepening?

hints.text: Look at the ratio k = K/L rather than the total capital stock K alone.
Capital deepening occurs only when capital grows faster than the workforce.

options_template.text: Any increase in the total dollar value of physical capital (K), even if the labor force grows faster than the capital stock.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Aggregate vs. Per-Worker Confusion): If L grows faster than K, capital per worker (K/L) actually falls (capital dilution), so no capital deepening occurs.

options_template.text: An increase in the amount of physical and human capital available per worker (k = K/L), which raises labor productivity (y = Y/L).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Equipping each worker with more machinery, computing tools, and training increases k = K/L and boosts output per worker.

options_template.text: A reduction in the annual depreciation rate achieved by shutting down older factories during a recession.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Idle Capacity Misconception): Shutting down factories lowers output rather than expanding capital available per employed worker.

options_template.text: A rise in household savings held exclusively in cash balances without any new equipment production.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Financial Hoarding Confusion): Holding cash does not increase physical or human capital per worker.

questions.title: Mechanism of Diminishing Marginal Returns to Capital
questions.prompt_template: Holding technology and worker skills constant, what does the principle of diminishing marginal returns to capital state?

hints.text: Think about giving a single farmer a first tractor, then a second tractor, then a third tractor.
Does total output fall, or does the *additional* output from each extra unit of capital get smaller?

options_template.text: Each additional dollar of physical capital per worker adds less incremental output per worker than the previous dollar added.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Diminishing marginal returns means marginal output remains positive as k rises, but each successive unit of capital adds a smaller boost to output per worker.

options_template.text: Adding more physical capital per worker immediately causes total output per worker to decline below zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Negative vs. Diminishing Returns): Diminishing marginal returns means output rises at a slower rate (smaller positive increments), not that total output immediately falls.

options_template.text: Physical capital wears out faster in high-income countries than in low-income countries.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Depreciation Confusion): Diminishing returns is a property of the production function holding technology fixed, not a statement about depreciation rates.

options_template.text: Doubling both physical capital and technology simultaneously always reduces labor productivity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ceteris Paribus Violation): Diminishing returns applies when technology and skills are held constant; technological progress shifts the production curve upward.

questions.title: Scope of Total Factor Productivity (Solow Residual)
questions.prompt_template: In the aggregate production framework Y* = A * f(K, L*), what does Total Factor Productivity (A)—often called the Solow residual—capture?

hints.text: Remember the Clear It Up note on the breadth of Robert Solow's productivity residual.
It includes everything that lets workers produce more output from the exact same stocks of capital and labor.

options_template.text: Only the number of physical machines installed in domestic manufacturing plants.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Capital Stock Conflation): Physical machines are counted in K, whereas A measures how efficiently K and L are combined.

options_template.text: Only a single breakthrough invention, excluding software, logistics, or management practices.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Narrow Invention Fallacy): Total Factor Productivity encompasses broad efficiency gains—including management, logistics, software, and institutions—not just one invention.

options_template.text: Broad efficiency gains—such as technological innovation, software automation, better management, logistics, and institutions—that yield more output from the same K and L.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Total Factor Productivity (A) captures all technological and organizational improvements that raise output without requiring extra physical capital or labor.

options_template.text: The percentage of the labor force that is temporarily unemployed during a recessionary gap.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cyclical Unemployment Confusion): Cyclical unemployment measures idle labor inside the PPF, not long-run technological efficiency A.

questions.title: Measuring Living Standards and Applying the Rule of 70
questions.prompt_template: Why do economists apply the Rule of 70 to real GDP per capita (Y/L) rather than raw aggregate GDP when comparing long-run living standards across nations?

hints.text: Think about what happens to average income if total GDP grows solely because the population grows at the same rate.
Distinguish aggregate economic size from output available per person.

options_template.text: Because the Rule of 70 mathematically fails whenever aggregate GDP exceeds $1 trillion.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Scale Myth): The Rule of 70 (70 / g) applies to any compounding variable regardless of dollar magnitude.

options_template.text: Because aggregate GDP ignores capital goods production, whereas real GDP per capita includes only consumer goods.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (GDP Composition Error): Both aggregate real GDP and real GDP per capita include consumer goods and capital goods; they differ by dividing by population/workers.

options_template.text: Because population growth always reduces real GDP per capita to zero over a 70-year period.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Malthusian Overstatement): Population growth dilutes aggregate gains only if output fails to keep pace; economies regularly grow per-capita income alongside population growth.

options_template.text: Because living standards depend on real output per person (Y/L); raw aggregate GDP can expand solely due to population growth without making the average person richer.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Dividing real output by population or workers isolates average prosperity, ensuring compound growth comparisons reflect genuine gains in living standards.

questions.title: Interpreting the Slope of the Linear Macroeconomic PPF
questions.prompt_template: In Figure 1, the baseline macroeconomic PPF is given by I = 400 - 0.5C (with Consumer Goods C on the horizontal axis and Capital Goods I on the vertical axis, in $ billions). What does the slope of -0.5 represent graphically?

hints.text: Recall that slope equals rise over run: Delta I / Delta C.
If C increases by +$1 billion along this line, how much does I change?

options_template.text: Producing an additional $1 billion of Consumer Goods requires sacrificing $0.5 billion of Capital Goods.
options_template.feedback: Correct. With I on the vertical axis and C on the horizontal axis, a slope of Delta I / Delta C = -0.5 means each +$1B of consumer goods costs $0.5B of capital goods.

options_template.text: Producing an additional $1 billion of Capital Goods requires sacrificing $0.5 billion of Consumer Goods.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Opportunity Cost): The inverse of the slope is 1 / 0.5 = 2, so +$1B of capital goods actually requires sacrificing $2B of consumer goods.

options_template.text: Half of the nation's existing physical capital stock depreciates every year.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Depreciation Confusion): The PPF slope reflects the static trade-off between producing C and I in one year, not the depreciation rate delta.

options_template.text: The economy is operating 50% inside its production frontier due to a recession.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Frontier vs. Interior Error): Points along the line I = 400 - 0.5C represent full-employment production on the frontier, not an interior recessionary gap.

questions.title: Comparing Future PPF Shifts for Bundle A vs. Bundle B
questions.prompt_template: Country A and Country B start on the exact same 2026 frontier (PPF_2026). Country A selects High-Consumption Bundle A (C = $600B, I = $100B), while Country B selects High-Investment Bundle B (C = $400B, I = $200B). Assuming both countries have identical depreciation below $100B, how do their 2036 frontiers compare graphically?

hints.text: Compare net investment (Delta K = I - delta * K) in Country B versus Country A.
Higher annual capital accumulation pushes the future PPF further outward along both axes.

options_template.text: Country A's 2036 PPF shifts further outward because higher current consumption stimulates more future factory capacity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Consumption-Led Capacity Fallacy): Consumer goods deliver immediate satisfaction but add nothing to future productive capacity; capital goods shift the frontier.

options_template.text: Country B's 2036 PPF shifts substantially further outward than Country A's because doubling capital goods production accelerates net capital accumulation.
options_template.feedback: Correct. By sacrificing $200B of current consumption to double gross investment to $200B, Country B builds a larger capital stock and pushes PPF_2036,B far beyond PPF_2036,A.

options_template.text: Both countries remain on the exact same 2036 PPF because they started with identical resources in 2026.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Static PPF Fallacy): A nation's choice along today's PPF alters tomorrow's capital stock and therefore shifts future PPFs at different speeds.

options_template.text: Country B's 2036 PPF shifts outward along the vertical (I) axis only, while its maximum Consumer Goods intercept stays fixed at $800B.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Single-Axis Shift Error): A larger physical capital stock raises productive capacity for both consumer goods and capital goods, shifting both intercepts outward.

questions.title: Graphical Outcome When Gross Investment Equals Depreciation
questions.prompt_template: Suppose an economy chooses a point on its macroeconomic PPF where gross capital goods production exactly equals annual depreciation (I = delta * K), with constant labor and technology. How does its PPF change from this year to next year?

hints.text: Compute net investment Delta K = I - delta * K when I = delta * K.
If the capital stock neither grows nor shrinks, what happens to productive capacity?

options_template.text: The PPF shifts outward steadily because gross investment is strictly positive.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Gross vs. Net Investment Confusion): Positive gross investment expands the frontier only if it exceeds depreciation (I > delta * K).

options_template.text: The PPF contracts inward because depreciation eliminates all newly produced consumer goods.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Depreciation Scope Error): Depreciation erodes physical capital, and here gross investment fully offsets it (Delta K = 0), so the frontier does not contract.

options_template.text: The PPF remains stationary in the exact same position because net investment is zero (Delta K = 0).
options_template.feedback: Correct. When new capital production merely replaces worn-out equipment, the capital stock is unchanged and the frontier neither expands nor contracts.

options_template.text: The PPF rotates clockwise, raising maximum Consumer Goods while lowering maximum Capital Goods.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unjustified Rotation): Zero net capital accumulation leaves total productive resources unchanged rather than tilting capacity toward consumer goods.

questions.title: Graphical Consequence of Under-Investment (I < delta * K)
questions.prompt_template: An economy devotes almost all of its resources to current consumer goods, choosing a point near the horizontal intercept of its macroeconomic PPF where gross investment falls below annual depreciation (I < delta * K). What happens to the economy's PPF over the next decade (holding labor and technology constant)?

hints.text: Determine the sign of Delta K = I - delta * K when I < delta * K.
Ask how a shrinking capital stock affects the maximum combinations of C and I the economy can produce.

options_template.text: The PPF shifts outward slowly because the economy is still operating efficiently on its frontier today.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Static Efficiency vs. Dynamic Growth): Operating on today's PPF means zero idle resources today, but if I < delta * K, the capital stock shrinks and future capacity falls.

options_template.text: The economy moves to an interior recessionary point, but the PPF curve itself stays fixed.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Idle Capacity vs. Shrinking Capital): Under-investment below depreciation physically erodes the capital stock, shifting the frontier inward rather than merely leaving factories idle.

options_template.text: The PPF stays fixed because depreciation only affects financial assets, not physical machinery.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Financial vs. Physical Depreciation): Depreciation measures physical wear, tear, and obsolescence of real machinery, buildings, and software.

options_template.text: The entire PPF shifts inward toward the origin because negative net investment shrinks the nation's physical capital stock.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When I < delta * K, net investment is negative (Delta K < 0), reducing the capital stock and shrinking maximum future production of both C and I.

questions.title: Identifying a Recessionary Output Gap on the Macro PPF
questions.prompt_template: On a macroeconomic PPF diagram with Consumer Goods (C) on the horizontal axis and Capital Goods (I) on the vertical axis, where is an economy located during a recessionary output gap (Y < Y*_1)?

hints.text: Remember that PPF_1 represents Potential GDP (Y*_1) at full-employment utilization.
If actual output Y is below Y*_1 due to idle factories and unemployed workers, is the point on, inside, or outside PPF_1?

options_template.text: At an interior point strictly inside PPF_1, reflecting idle labor and underutilized factories.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Point R inside PPF_1 illustrates that the economy is producing below its full-employment potential (Y < Y*_1) even though its physical frontier remains intact.

options_template.text: Directly on the vertical intercept of PPF_1, where Consumer Goods equal zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Intercept Confusion): Any point on PPF_1 represents full employment of resources, not a recessionary output gap.

options_template.text: At a point temporarily outside PPF_1, where factories run unsustainable overtime shifts.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Overheating Reversal): Operating temporarily outside PPF_1 depicts overheating (Y > Y*_1), not a recessionary gap.

options_template.text: On a newly shifted outer frontier PPF_2 above PPF_1.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Secular Growth Confusion): Moving to PPF_2 represents long-run expansion of Potential GDP, not a cyclical downturn.

questions.title: Representing Short-Run Cyclical Recovery on the PPF
questions.prompt_template: In Figure 2, Stage 1 draws an arrow from interior Point R (Y < Y*_1) outward to Point E_1 on the existing curve PPF_1 (Y = Y*_1). What macroeconomic process does this arrow depict?

hints.text: Notice that the frontier PPF_1 itself has NOT shifted during Stage 1.
What happens when unemployed workers are rehired and idle assembly lines restart?

options_template.text: Long-run secular economic growth driven by technological breakthroughs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Recovery vs. Secular Growth): Secular growth shifts the entire frontier outward (PPF_1 -> PPF_2); Stage 1 moves back to the existing frontier.

options_template.text: Short-run cyclical recovery closing a recessionary output gap by putting idle resources back to work.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Moving from interior Point R to Point E_1 on PPF_1 eliminates the negative output gap and restores full-employment output Y = Y*_1.

options_template.text: Inflationary overheating caused by pushing factories beyond normal sustainable capacity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Overheating Misidentification): Overheating pushes the economy beyond PPF_1 (Y > Y*_1), whereas R -> E_1 only restores normal full capacity.

options_template.text: A movement along PPF_1 that sacrifices Consumer Goods to produce more Capital Goods.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Along-Curve Trade-Off Confusion): Moving from interior Point R to E_1 can increase both C and I simultaneously because idle resources are being re-employed.

questions.title: Representing Long-Run Secular Growth on the PPF
questions.prompt_template: In Figure 2, Stage 2 shows the economy moving from Point E_1 on PPF_1 to Point E_2 on a new outer curve PPF_2. Which combination of factors can generate this graphical shift?

hints.text: Look at the production function for Potential GDP: Y* = A * f(K, L*).
Distinguish supply-side capacity expanders from short-run demand-side stimulus.

options_template.text: Emergency fiscal stimulus checks and lower interest rates while capital stock, labor, and technology remain fixed.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Only Growth Fallacy): Fiscal and monetary stimulus reopen idle factories (R -> E_1) but cannot shift Potential GDP (PPF_1 -> PPF_2) with fixed inputs and technology.

options_template.text: Rehiring cyclically unemployed workers who were laid off during a recent downturn.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cyclical Recovery Confusion): Rehiring cyclically unemployed workers moves the economy from inside PPF_1 to E_1; it does not shift PPF_1 to PPF_2.

options_template.text: Sustained net capital deepening, human capital investment, and higher Total Factor Productivity (A).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Expanding physical capital, workforce skills, and technological efficiency raises Potential GDP from Y*_1 to Y*_2, shifting the entire frontier outward to PPF_2.

options_template.text: Running existing factories on unsustainable weekend overtime shifts for two consecutive quarters.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Temporary Overheating Confusion): Unsustainable overtime creates a temporary surge beyond PPF_1 rather than a permanent outward shift to PPF_2.

questions.title: Locating Temporary Overheating on the Macro PPF Diagram
questions.prompt_template: During a rapid demand surge (such as the 2021–2022 U.S. reopening), factories run unsustainable overtime shifts and supply chains face acute bottlenecks. Where is the economy operating relative to its normal sustainable frontier PPF_1?

hints.text: Recall that PPF_1 represents normal sustainable full-employment output Y*_1, not a hard physical ceiling.
Compare actual output Y with Potential GDP Y*_1 during overheating.

options_template.text: Deep inside PPF_1, because bottlenecks reduce employment below normal levels.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Recessionary Gap Confusion): Bottlenecks during a demand surge reflect strained over-utilization (Y > Y*_1), not idle capacity inside PPF_1.

options_template.text: Exactly at the origin (0, 0), because supply chains have completely halted.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Extreme Literalism): Overheating occurs when output is exceptionally high—above Y*_1—not zero.

options_template.text: Permanently on a new outer frontier PPF_2 with zero inflationary pressure.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Permanent Capacity Confusion): Demand-driven overheating is temporary and inflationary, unlike permanent secular growth to PPF_2.

options_template.text: At a point temporarily outside PPF_1 (Y > Y*_1), which cannot be sustained without generating inflationary pressure.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because Y* is normal sustainable capacity rather than an absolute physical wall, intense demand can briefly push actual output beyond PPF_1, fueling inflation.

questions.title: Graphical Shape of the Per-Worker Production Function y(k)
questions.prompt_template: On a graph with Capital per Worker (k = K/L) on the horizontal axis and Output per Worker (y = Y/L) on the vertical axis, why does the per-worker production curve y_0(k) slope upward but flatten out as k increases?

hints.text: Connect the slope of y_0(k) to the marginal product of capital per worker.
A positive slope means more capital raises output; a flattening slope means each extra unit adds less than the previous unit.

options_template.text: Additional capital per worker raises labor productivity (positive slope), but diminishing marginal returns cause each successive dollar of capital to yield a smaller output gain (flattening slope).
options_template.feedback: Correct. The concave upward-sloping curve directly visualizes positive marginal product of capital combined with diminishing marginal returns, holding technology constant.

options_template.text: Additional capital per worker lowers labor productivity once k passes $25k, causing the curve to bend downward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Negative Slope Fallacy): Diminishing marginal returns flattens the upward slope toward zero; it does not make the curve slope downward.

options_template.text: The curve flattens because Total Factor Productivity (A) automatically declines whenever workers receive better tools.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ceteris Paribus Error): Along a single curve y_0(k), Total Factor Productivity A_0 is held constant; the flattening comes from diminishing returns to capital.

options_template.text: The curve is a straight line with constant slope because every extra tractor adds the exact same amount of grain.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Constant Returns Assumption): A straight line would imply constant marginal returns to capital, contradicting diminishing marginal returns.

questions.title: Interpreting Equal-Output Steps Along y_0(k)
questions.prompt_template: In Figure 3, along baseline curve y_0(k), raising output per worker by +$50k from $50k to $100k requires adding +$75k of capital per worker (from k = $25k to k = $100k). Raising output per worker by another +$50k (from $100k to $150k) requires adding +$125k of capital per worker (from k = $100k to k = $225k). What does this graphical comparison prove?

hints.text: Compare the capital injection required for the first +$50k of output versus the second +$50k of output.
Because the required Delta k increases from +$75k to +$125k for the same Delta y = +$50k, what is happening to the marginal return on capital?

options_template.text: Capital deepening becomes progressively more productive at higher levels of capital per worker.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Increasing Returns Reversal): Needing *more* capital (+$125k vs. +$75k) to achieve the exact same +$50k output gain proves productivity per incremental dollar is falling, not rising.

options_template.text: Holding technology constant, diminishing marginal returns force an economy to inject progressively larger amounts of capital per worker to achieve each equal gain in output per worker.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Requiring +$125k instead of +$75k of extra capital per worker for the same +$50k output boost is the exact graphical signature of diminishing marginal returns.

options_template.text: Technological progress (A) shifted the curve downward between k = $100k and k = $225k.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift vs. Movement Confusion): All three points lie along the same baseline curve y_0(k) with unchanged technology A_0.

options_template.text: The economy entered a recessionary output gap once capital per worker exceeded $100k.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Business Cycle Confusion): Moving rightward along y_0(k) represents long-run capital deepening, not a short-run recessionary output gap.

questions.topic: Movement Along vs. Shift of y(k)
questions.title: Capital Deepening vs. Technological Progress on the y(k) Graph
questions.prompt_template: On the per-worker production graph plotting y = Y/L against k = K/L, how do capital deepening and an increase in Total Factor Productivity (A) differ graphically?

hints.text: Ask which variable is on the horizontal axis (k) and which variable is a shift parameter (A).
Changing a variable on an axis moves along the curve; changing an external parameter shifts the entire curve.

options_template.text: Capital deepening shifts the entire y(k) curve upward, whereas higher Total Factor Productivity causes a movement rightward along y_0(k).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift-Movement Reversal): This swaps the two effects; k is on the horizontal axis so changing k moves along the curve, whereas changing A shifts the curve.

options_template.text: Both capital deepening and higher Total Factor Productivity shift the y(k) curve downward toward the horizontal axis.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direction Error): Both capital deepening and technological progress raise output per worker rather than lowering it.

options_template.text: Capital deepening moves the economy rightward along the existing curve y_0(k), whereas higher Total Factor Productivity shifts the entire curve upward from y_0(k) to y_1(k).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Increasing k moves along y_0(k) subject to diminishing returns, while raising A lifts output per worker at every level of k.

options_template.text: Neither factor changes the graph because output per worker is fixed by the size of the population.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-Productivity Myth): Output per worker rises through both capital deepening (movement along) and TFP gains (upward shift).

questions.title: Interpreting a Vertical Jump on the Per-Worker Production Graph
questions.prompt_template: In Figure 3, at a constant capital per worker of k = $100k, a vertical arrow points directly upward from y = $100k on y_0(k) to y = $130k on y_1(k). What economic event does this vertical jump represent?

hints.text: Notice that k = $100k did NOT change—the arrow is strictly vertical.
How can workers produce $30k more output each using the exact same dollar value of machinery per worker?

options_template.text: An increase in physical machinery per worker with no change in software or management.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Capital Deepening Misidentification): Adding more physical machinery per worker would increase k (moving rightward), whereas here k stays fixed at $100k.

options_template.text: A decrease in the annual depreciation rate that lowers the replacement cost of equipment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Depreciation Confusion): Lower depreciation affects net capital accumulation over time, not output produced from a given current stock k.

options_template.text: A rise in consumer goods prices that inflates nominal output per worker by 30%.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Nominal vs. Real Illusion): The vertical axis measures real output per worker (y = Y/L), not nominal price inflation.

options_template.text: An increase in Total Factor Productivity (A_0 -> A_1) that allows workers to produce $30k more real output per worker from the exact same capital per worker.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A purely vertical shift at fixed k = $100k isolates technological, software, or organizational progress (higher A) that lifts output without additional capital deepening.

questions.title: Graphical Effect of a Higher Saving Rate in the Solow Model
questions.prompt_template: In the Solow Neoclassical Growth Model, steady-state capital per worker (k*) occurs where gross investment per worker, i = s * A * k^alpha, equals break-even depreciation and workforce dilution, (delta + n)k. Graphically, what happens when the national saving rate (s) rises permanently?

hints.text: Identify which of the two curves contains the saving rate s.
When s increases, the investment curve s * A * k^alpha shifts upward while the straight break-even line (delta + n)k stays unchanged.

options_template.text: The investment curve s * A * k^alpha shifts upward, moving its intersection with the break-even line (delta + n)k to a higher steady-state capital per worker (k*) and higher output per worker (y*).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Raising s lifts investment per worker above break-even at the old k*, causing Delta k > 0 until the economy converges to a permanently higher k* and y*.

options_template.text: The straight break-even line (delta + n)k pivots upward, reducing steady-state capital per worker k*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Curve Shifted): The break-even line depends on depreciation (delta) and labor growth (n), not on the saving rate s.

options_template.text: Both curves shift downward simultaneously, leaving steady-state capital per worker k* unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direction and Scope Error): Higher saving increases investment per worker rather than lowering either curve.

options_template.text: The investment curve becomes a vertical line, causing capital per worker to grow infinitely without ever reaching a steady state.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Diminishing Returns): Because 0 < alpha < 1, the shifted investment curve still flattens and intersects the linear break-even line at a finite new k*.

questions.title: Calculating Capital Goods Output Along a Linear Macro PPF
questions.prompt_template: An economy's linear macroeconomic PPF is described by I = 500 - 0.25C, where Consumer Goods (C) and Capital Goods (I) are measured in billions of dollars. If the nation reduces Consumer Goods production from C = $1,200 billion to C = $800 billion, what is its new level of Capital Goods production (I)?

hints.text: Substitute the new value C = 800 directly into the PPF equation I = 500 - 0.25C.
Be careful to report the new total level of I, not just the change in I.

options_template.text: $100 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Change vs. Level Error): Cutting C by $400B increases I by +$100B (from $200B to $300B), so $100B is the gain (Delta I), not the new total level of Capital Goods.

options_template.text: $300 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. Substituting C = 800 into I = 500 - 0.25C yields I = 500 - 0.25(800) = 500 - 200 = $300 billion.

options_template.text: $200 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Initial Value Error): $200 billion is the initial Capital Goods output at C = $1,200B (500 - 0.25 * 1,200), before reallocating resources toward investment.

options_template.text: $400 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (One-for-One Trade-Off Error): $400 billion is the reduction in Consumer Goods (1,200 - 800), ignoring the slope of -0.25 that converts $400B of C into $100B of additional I.

questions.title: Calculating Year 2 Capital Stock with Positive Net Investment
questions.prompt_template: A nation begins Year 1 with a physical capital stock of K_1 = $8,000 billion and an annual depreciation rate of delta = 5% (0.05). If Year 1 gross investment is I_1 = $650 billion, what is the nation's Year 2 capital stock (K_2)?

hints.text: First calculate annual depreciation: delta * K_1 = 0.05 * $8,000 billion.
Next compute net investment (Delta K = I_1 - delta * K_1) and add it to K_1.

options_template.text: $8,650 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Depreciation): Adding full gross investment ($8,000B + $650B) omits the $400B of existing capital that wore out during Year 1.

options_template.text: $7,600 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitting Gross Investment): Subtracting depreciation alone ($8,000B - $400B) ignores the $650B of newly produced capital goods.

options_template.text: $8,250 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. Annual depreciation is 0.05 * $8,000B = $400B, so net investment is Delta K = $650B - $400B = +$250B, giving K_2 = $8,000B + $250B = $8,250 billion.

options_template.text: $8,400 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Adding Depreciation Error): Adding depreciation ($400B) to K_1 instead of net investment ($250B) confuses wear-and-tear with capital accumulation.

questions.title: Calculating Year 2 Capital Stock When Depreciation Exceeds Investment
questions.prompt_template: An economy begins Year 1 with a physical capital stock of K_1 = $6,000 billion and an annual depreciation rate of delta = 7.5% (0.075). If Year 1 gross investment is only I_1 = $360 billion, what is the Year 2 capital stock (K_2)?

hints.text: Calculate annual depreciation first: delta * K_1 = 0.075 * $6,000 billion.
Compare I_1 to delta * K_1—if depreciation is larger, net investment Delta K is negative.

options_template.text: $6,360 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Depreciation): Adding gross investment ($6,000B + $360B) ignores the $450B of capital lost to wear and obsolescence.

options_template.text: $6,090 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Reversal Error): Because depreciation ($450B) exceeds gross investment ($360B), net investment is -$90B, not +$90B.

options_template.text: $5,550 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitting Gross Investment): Subtracting $450B of depreciation without crediting the $360B of new gross investment understates Year 2 capital.

options_template.text: $5,910 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. Annual depreciation is 0.075 * $6,000B = $450B, yielding net investment Delta K = $360B - $450B = -$90B and K_2 = $6,000B - $90B = $5,910 billion.

questions.title: Finding the Break-Even Maintenance Investment Threshold
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a country starts the year with a physical capital stock of K_1 = $12,500 billion and an annual depreciation rate of delta = 4% (0.04). What is the minimum level of gross investment (I_min) required simply to prevent its macroeconomic PPF from contracting?

hints.text: To prevent contraction, net investment must be at least zero: Delta K = I_1 - delta * K_1 >= 0.
Set I_min = delta * K_1 and convert 4% carefully to 0.04.

options_template.text: $500 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. Break-even maintenance investment equals annual depreciation: I_min = 0.04 * $12,500B = $500 billion.

options_template.text: $50 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Decimal Place Error): Multiplying by 0.004 instead of 0.04 understates required maintenance investment by a factor of ten.

options_template.text: $5,000 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Decimal Place Error): Multiplying by 0.40 instead of 0.04 overstates annual depreciation by a factor of ten.

options_template.text: $12,000 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Remaining Stock Confusion): $12,000 billion is the surviving capital stock (1 - delta) * K_1 after depreciation, not the annual depreciation replacement requirement.

questions.title: Calculating the Percentage Recessionary Output Gap
questions.prompt_template: Suppose an economy's Potential GDP along PPF_1 is Y* = $20.0 trillion, but a recession pushes actual real GDP inside the frontier to Y = $19.2 trillion. What is the economy's percentage output gap?

hints.text: Use the canonical formula: Percentage Output Gap = ((Y - Y*) / Y*) * 100%.
Check both the sign (negative when Y < Y*) and the denominator (Potential GDP Y*, not actual Y).

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Reversal Error): Because actual real GDP ($19.2T) is below Potential GDP ($20.0T), the output gap is negative (-4.0%), not positive.
Correct. The dollar output gap is $19.2T - $20.0T = -$0.8T, and dividing by Potential GDP gives (-0.8 / 20.0) * 100% = -4.0%.
Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Denominator Error): Dividing -$0.8T by actual GDP ($19.2T) instead of Potential GDP ($20.0T) miscalculates the percentage output gap.
Diagnostic fallacy (Dollar vs. Percentage Confusion): -$0.8 trillion is the dollar output gap, not the percentage deviation from Potential GDP.

questions.title: Computing New Potential GDP (Y*_2) After Secular Expansion
questions.prompt_template: An economy has current Potential GDP of Y*_1 = $16.0 trillion, while a temporary downturn has pushed actual real GDP to Y = $15.2 trillion. If capital deepening and Total Factor Productivity gains expand Potential GDP by 2.5% over the coming year, what is the new Potential GDP (Y*_2) along PPF_2?

hints.text: Secular growth expands Potential GDP (Y*_1), not recessionary actual output (Y).
Multiply Y*_1 = $16.0 trillion by (1 + 0.025).

options_template.text: $15.58 trillion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Recessionary Base Error): Applying the 2.5% growth rate to recessionary actual GDP ($15.2T * 1.025) confuses cyclical output with Potential GDP.

options_template.text: $18.5 trillion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Percentage-to-Trillions Addition Error): Adding 2.5 directly to $16.0T treats a 2.5% rate as a $2.5 trillion lump sum.

options_template.text: $16.4 trillion
options_template.feedback: Correct. Expanding baseline Potential GDP by 2.5% gives Y*_2 = $16.0T * 1.025 = $16.4 trillion.

options_template.text: $16.8 trillion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Adding Output Gap Error): Adding the $0.8T recessionary gap on top of $16.0T confuses cyclical recovery back to Y*_1 with secular frontier expansion.

questions.title: Calculating Percentage Capital Deepening (k = K/L)
questions.prompt_template: Over a five-year span, a nation's physical capital stock expands from K_0 = $1,200 billion to K_1 = $1,800 billion, while its workforce grows from L_0 = 15 million to L_1 = 18 million workers. What is the percentage increase in capital per worker (k = K/L)?

hints.text: Convert billions to millions (e.g., $1,200 billion = $1,200,000 million) to compute k_0 = K_0 / L_0 and k_1 = K_1 / L_1.
Then compute the percentage change: ((k_1 - k_0) / k_0) * 100%.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Labor Growth): +50.0% is the growth rate of the aggregate capital stock K alone ($600B / $1,200B), ignoring that the workforce also grew by 20%.
Diagnostic fallacy (Linear Subtraction Approximation Error): Subtracting 20% labor growth from 50% capital growth yields +30%, which ignores exact ratio compounding (1.50 / 1.20 = 1.25).
Diagnostic fallacy (Ending-Base Denominator Error): Dividing the $20,000 gain by the ending value k_1 = $100,000 instead of the initial value k_0 = $80,000 understates the percentage increase.
Correct. Initial capital per worker is k_0 = $1,200,000M / 15M = $80,000 and new capital per worker is k_1 = $1,800,000M / 18M = $100,000, an exact increase of ($20,000 / $80,000) * 100% = +25.0%.

questions.title: Calculating Output per Worker After a TFP Gain
questions.prompt_template: Suppose an economy's per-worker production function is y = A * sqrt(k), where k and y are measured in thousands of dollars ($k). Initially, Total Factor Productivity is A_0 = 10 and capital per worker is k = $100k, giving y_0 = $100k. If technological progress raises Total Factor Productivity to A_1 = 12 while k remains fixed at $100k, what is the new output per worker (y_1)?

hints.text: Evaluate sqrt(k) first for k = 100.
Multiply the new TFP level A_1 = 12 by sqrt(100).

options_template.feedback: Correct. Since sqrt(100) = 10, substituting A_1 = 12 gives y_1 = 12 * 10 = $120k per worker.
Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Square Root Error): Multiplying 12 * 100 = $1,200k forgets the square root representing diminishing marginal returns to capital.
Diagnostic fallacy (Additive TFP Error): Adding the change in A (+2) directly to y_0 ($100k) treats Total Factor Productivity as additive rather than multiplicative.
Diagnostic fallacy (Squaring A Error): Computing 12^2 = $144k squares Total Factor Productivity instead of multiplying A_1 by sqrt(k) = 10.

questions.title: Applying the Rule of 70 Without the Decimal Trap
questions.prompt_template: If an economy's real GDP per capita grows steadily at 2.5% per year, approximately how many years will it take for average living standards to double according to the Rule of 70?

hints.text: Use Doubling Years ≈ 70 / g.
Remember the Clear It Up warning: enter g as the percentage number (2.5), NOT as the decimal 0.025.

options_template.text: 2,800 years
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Decimal Trap): Dividing 70 by the decimal 0.025 instead of the percentage number 2.5 inflates the doubling time by a factor of 100.

options_template.text: 28 years
options_template.feedback: Correct. Entering the percentage growth rate g = 2.5 into the Rule of 70 gives 70 / 2.5 = 28 years.

options_template.text: 40 years
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Rule of 100 / Linear Growth Error): Computing 100 / 2.5 = 40 years ignores compounding; simple interest takes 40 years to double, whereas compound growth doubles in 28 years.

options_template.text: 1.75 years
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Multiplication Instead of Division): Multiplying 70 * 0.025 = 1.75 inverts the Rule of 70 relationship.

questions.title: Projecting Multi-Decade Income via Repeated Doublings
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a developing economy begins with real GDP per capita of $15,000 and sustains an annual growth rate of 5.0% per year for 42 years. Using the Rule of 70, approximately what will its real GDP per capita be after 42 years?

hints.text: Step 1: Find the doubling time (70 / 5.0) and count how many doublings fit into 42 years.
Step 2: Apply compound doubling (2^m), NOT linear multiplication (2 * m).

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Linear Doubling Fallacy): Multiplying $15,000 by (2 * 3) = 6 treats three doublings linearly; compound growth multiplies by 2^3 = 8.
Diagnostic fallacy (Additive Count Fallacy): Multiplying $15,000 by 3 (the number of doublings) ignores that each doubling multiplies the entire accumulated income by 2.
Correct. Doubling time is 70 / 5.0 = 14 years, yielding 42 / 14 = 3 doublings; compounding multiplies income by 2^3 = 8, so $15,000 * 8 = $120,000.
Diagnostic fallacy (Miscounted Doublings): Multiplying by 2^2 = 4 accounts for only 28 years (2 doublings) rather than the full 42-year span (3 doublings).

questions.title: Applying the Exact Compound Growth Formula Y_n = Y_0(1 + r)^n
questions.prompt_template: If a nation's real GDP per capita is $40,000 today and grows at an exact rate of 5% per year (r = 0.05) for 2 years, what is its exact real GDP per capita after 2 years?

hints.text: Use the exact compound formula Y_n = Y_0 * (1 + r)^n with Y_0 = 40,000, r = 0.05, and n = 2.
Notice that Year 2's 5% gain applies to the Year 1 income of $42,000, not just the original $40,000.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Simple Interest / Linear Math Error): Computing $40,000 * (1 + 2 * 0.05) = $44,000 omits the $100 of compounding earned in Year 2 on Year 1's $2,000 gain.
Diagnostic fallacy (Single-Period Error): $42,000 = $40,000 * 1.05 reflects only 1 year of growth rather than 2 years.
Diagnostic fallacy (Doubled Annual Rate Error): Computing $40,000 * (1.10)^2 erroneously doubles the annual growth rate to 10% per year before squaring.

questions.title: Solving for Solow Steady-State Capital and Output per Worker
questions.prompt_template: In the Solow Neoclassical Growth Model with y = A * k^0.5 (alpha = 0.5), suppose the saving rate is s = 0.30, Total Factor Productivity is A = 1.0, depreciation is delta = 0.04, and labor force growth is n = 0.02. Using k* = (sA / (delta + n))^(1 / (1 - alpha)) and y* = A * (k*)^alpha, what are steady-state capital per worker (k*) and output per worker (y*)?

hints.text: First compute the ratio sA / (delta + n) = (0.30 * 1.0) / (0.04 + 0.02).
Since alpha = 0.5, the exponent 1 / (1 - alpha) equals 2, so k* = (ratio)^2 and y* = A * sqrt(k*).

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Exponent Error): Setting k* = sA / (delta + n) = 5.0 forgets to raise the ratio to the power 1 / (1 - 0.5) = 2.
Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Labor Growth Dilution): Dividing 0.30 by delta = 0.04 alone ignores workforce growth (n = 0.02) in the break-even denominator (delta + n).
Diagnostic fallacy (Linear Alpha Error): Multiplying k* by 0.5 (25.0 * 0.5 = 12.5) instead of raising k* to the 0.5 power (sqrt(25.0) = 5.0) misapplies the Cobb-Douglas exponent.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Explaining the Post-1960 Divergence Between South Korea and Ghana
questions.prompt_template: In 1960, South Korea and Ghana had virtually identical real GDP per capita (roughly $1,200 in modern PPP dollars), yet over the next six decades South Korea's per-capita income surpassed $35,000 while Ghana's grew far more slowly. Which macroeconomic mechanism best explains this divergence?

hints.text: Connect the Bring It Home case to the intertemporal PPF choice and Total Factor Productivity.
Ask what happens when one nation consistently maintains I > delta * K and adopts advanced technology over decades.

options_template.text: South Korea relied exclusively on short-run fiscal stimulus checks to keep its economy operating inside its original 1960 PPF.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Stimulus-Driven Growth Fallacy): Short-run demand stimulus closes cyclical gaps but cannot multiply living standards nearly thirtyfold over six decades.

options_template.text: South Korea devoted a large share of output to physical infrastructure, industrial equipment, and human capital above annual depreciation while raising Total Factor Productivity, repeatedly shifting its PPF outward.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Sustained net capital accumulation (I > delta * K), capital deepening, and technological adoption compounded over six decades to transform South Korea's productive frontier.

options_template.text: South Korea eliminated all household consumption (C = 0) for sixty years so that 100% of GDP went into financial stock purchases.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Consumption & Financial Investment Fallacy): Zero consumption is physically impossible, and buying financial stocks does not expand real productive capacity.

options_template.text: Ghana suffered a permanent recessionary output gap for sixty years while its underlying PPF grew identically to South Korea's.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cyclical vs. Secular Confusion): A multi-decade gap exceeding an order of magnitude reflects divergent secular frontier growth (Y*), not a 60-year cyclical recession.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Policy Trade-Offs in Grid Modernization and AI Compute Buildouts
questions.prompt_template: A nation operating on its macroeconomic PPF launches a massive buildout of high-voltage electrical grid transformers and hyperscale AI data centers. Using the intertemporal PPF framework, what is the immediate macroeconomic opportunity cost and the long-run objective of this reallocation?

hints.text: Identify what scarce resources (engineers, steel, electricity, construction crews) must be diverted today.
Connect today's sacrifice in C to tomorrow's expansion in productive capacity.

options_template.text: There is zero opportunity cost today because data centers are financed with corporate bonds rather than physical resources.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Free-Lunch / Financial Illusion): Regardless of financing, building real power grids and servers requires scarce engineers, materials, and crews that cannot simultaneously produce consumer goods.

options_template.text: The economy permanently shifts its PPF inward because energy infrastructure is classified as a consumer good.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Misclassification of Capital Goods): Power-grid transformers and compute servers are durable capital goods that expand future output, not consumer goods.

options_template.text: Diverting engineers, materials, and construction crews reduces current Consumer Goods output (such as residential housing) today in order to expand durable capital and shift the future PPF outward.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because resources are finite along the PPF, prioritizing grid and compute infrastructure sacrifices current consumption to build durable assets that raise future productive capacity.

options_template.text: The buildout immediately pushes the economy into a recessionary output gap inside PPF_1 by leaving construction crews idle.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reallocation vs. Idleness): Moving along the PPF reallocates fully employed resources from C to I; it does not leave resources idle.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Demand Stimulus Cannot Substitute for Secular Growth Policy
questions.prompt_template: During a deep recession, policymakers enact temporary tax cuts and interest-rate reductions that successfully restore full employment. A commentator argues that repeating these exact stimulus measures every year at full employment will permanently double the nation's long-run economic growth rate. Why is this argument flawed?

hints.text: Distinguish moving from R to E_1 (closing a gap) from shifting PPF_1 to PPF_2 (raising Y*).
Consider what happens when aggregate demand is stimulated once the economy is already operating on its PPF (Y = Y*).

options_template.text: Because fiscal and monetary stimulus never affect aggregate spending even during a recession.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ineffectiveness Overstatement): Countercyclical stimulus does help restore aggregate spending during recessions (R -> E_1); its limitation is at or above Potential GDP.

options_template.text: Because tax cuts and lower interest rates automatically shrink the nation's physical capital stock by increasing depreciation.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Depreciation Mechanism Error): Stimulus does not physically accelerate machine wear-and-tear; it simply fails to create permanent supply-side capacity when resources are already fully employed.

options_template.text: Because Potential GDP is fixed forever and no public policy can ever influence long-run growth.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Growth Fatalism): Supply-side policies—such as education, R&D grants, and infrastructure—do raise Potential GDP over time.

options_template.text: Because demand stimulus closes recessionary gaps by reopening idle capacity (R -> E_1), but once at full employment it merely causes inflationary overheating (Y > Y*) rather than shifting the PPF outward.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Stimulus checks reopen factories rather than frontiers; sustained outward shifts in Y* require capital deepening, human capital, and Total Factor Productivity.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Diagnosing Recent U.S. Output Gap Regimes
questions.prompt_template: Comparing the U.S. economy during 2009–2015 (following the 2008–2009 financial crisis) with 2021–2022 (reopening amid rapid fiscal and monetary stimulus), how should macroeconomists classify these two episodes relative to Potential GDP (Y*)?

hints.text: Recall the U.S. Output Gaps case study in Section 2.2.
Match persistent idle factories/unemployment to Y < Y* and supply-chain bottlenecks/inflation to Y > Y*.

options_template.text: 2009–2015 reflected a persistent negative output gap inside the PPF (Y < Y*), whereas 2021–2022 reflected temporary overheating above normal sustainable capacity (Y > Y*) with bottlenecks and inflation.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The post-crisis slump gradually reabsorbed idle workers and plants inside PPF_1, whereas the 2021–2022 demand surge briefly strained capacity above Y*, fueling inflation.

options_template.text: 2009–2015 reflected inflationary overheating above the PPF (Y > Y*), whereas 2021–2022 reflected a persistent recessionary output gap (Y < Y*).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Episode Reversal): The 2009–2015 period was marked by high unemployment and slack (Y < Y*), while 2021–2022 was marked by excess demand and bottlenecks (Y > Y*).

options_template.text: Both episodes occurred strictly on the frontier (Y = Y*) because the U.S. economy never deviates from Potential GDP.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Continuous Full-Employment Fallacy): Business cycles routinely push actual real GDP below or temporarily above Potential GDP.

options_template.text: Both episodes were caused solely by negative net investment contracting the physical PPF inward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Structural Contraction Conflation): Both episodes primarily reflected cyclical deviations of aggregate spending relative to Y*, not physical destruction of the frontier.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Diagnosing Deteriorating Public Infrastructure Despite Positive Spending
questions.prompt_template: A government agency proudly reports that it spent $120 billion this year on highway repairs, bridges, and electrical grid upgrades—confirming positive gross infrastructure investment (I > 0). Yet engineers document that overall infrastructure quality and capacity declined over the same year. Which economic diagnosis resolves this apparent paradox?

hints.text: Compare gross investment ($120 billion) against annual physical depreciation (delta * K) of the existing infrastructure stock.
Can an asset base shrink while new spending is positive?

options_template.text: The engineers must be mistaken, because any positive gross investment guarantees an expanding capital stock.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Gross = Net Fallacy): Positive gross investment still yields a shrinking capital stock whenever wear-and-tear exceeds new outlays.

options_template.text: Annual wear, tear, and obsolescence (delta * K) on existing bridges, roads, and grids exceeded $120 billion, making net investment negative (Delta K < 0).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Even with $120B of gross spending, if annual depreciation exceeds $120B, net capital accumulation is negative and the nation's physical infrastructure erodes.

options_template.text: Highway and power-grid spending counts as consumer goods rather than capital goods, so it cannot affect the capital stock.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Asset Misclassification): Bridges, transit, and power lines are core physical capital goods.

options_template.text: The economy experienced diminishing marginal returns to consumption, which automatically erased the $120 billion in repairs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Irrelevant Mechanism): Physical deterioration despite positive gross outlays is explained by I < delta * K, not by diminishing returns to consumption.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Subsidizing Physical Machinery Alone Eventually Stalls Per-Capita Growth
questions.prompt_template: An advanced economy attempts to sustain 4% annual growth in real GDP per capita indefinitely solely by subsidizing firms to buy ever more physical machinery per worker, while investing nothing in research, education, or organizational innovation. Based on the macroeconomic growth model, why will this investment-only strategy eventually fail?

hints.text: Think about moving further and further right along a single concave production curve y_0(k).
What happens to incremental output per extra machine relative to its depreciation cost?

options_template.text: Because physical machinery never raises labor productivity even in early stages of development.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Early-Stage Denial): Capital deepening strongly raises labor productivity initially (steep portion of y_0(k)); the constraint binds as k becomes very large.

options_template.text: Because buying more physical machinery shifts the y(k) curve downward by reducing Total Factor Productivity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Shift Direction): Buying machinery moves the economy rightward along y_0(k); it does not shift A downward.

options_template.text: Because diminishing marginal returns to capital cause each extra dollar of machinery to yield smaller output gains until additional machines barely cover their own depreciation, requiring Total Factor Productivity (A) for sustained growth.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Without technological and organizational progress (A) shifting y(k) upward, diminishing returns eventually limit capital-only growth to a stationary steady state.

options_template.text: Because subsidies for physical machinery automatically trigger a recessionary output gap inside the PPF.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cyclical Confusion): The limit on investment-only growth is a long-run supply-side constraint (diminishing returns), not a short-run demand deficiency.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Matching Public Growth Policies to Production Function Channels
questions.prompt_template: A policy committee proposes three long-run growth initiatives: (1) expanding public and higher education, (2) funding scientific R&D grants with patent protection, and (3) modernizing ports and power grids. How do these three levers primarily raise long-run real GDP per capita?

hints.text: Recall the three channels in the Growth Policy Levers case study: human capital, Total Factor Productivity (A), and physical infrastructure.
Check which lever specifically shifts the y(k) curve upward via technological breakthroughs.

options_template.text: All three levers work solely by increasing short-run household consumption during recessions.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Short-Run Demand Confusion): Education, R&D, and infrastructure are long-run supply-side levers that expand Potential GDP (Y*).

options_template.text: Education and ports raise Total Factor Productivity exclusively, while R&D grants only prevent machinery from depreciating.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Channel Misattribution): R&D and patents are the primary drivers of scientific breakthroughs lifting TFP (A), whereas education deepens human capital and ports deepen physical infrastructure.

options_template.text: All three levers lower capital per worker so that the economy avoids diminishing marginal returns.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Anti-Capital Fallacy): Lowering k reduces output per worker; growth policies aim to deepen physical/human capital while shifting y(k) upward via higher A.

options_template.text: Education deepens human capital, R&D grants and patents lift Total Factor Productivity (A) through innovation, and ports and power grids deepen physical infrastructure to lower costs across industries.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Together these three supply-side channels expand capital per worker, human skill, and technological efficiency, shifting both y(k) and the macroeconomic PPF outward.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why a 1.5-Percentage-Point Growth Gap Transforms National Wealth
questions.prompt_template: Two economies start in 2026 with identical real GDP per capita of $20,000. Country X adopts policies yielding 2.0% annual per-capita growth, whereas Country Y adopts productivity reforms yielding 3.5% annual growth. Over a 70-year human lifetime (to 2096), why is a seemingly modest 1.5-percentage-point annual difference so consequential?

hints.text: Compare doubling times via the Rule of 70: 70 / 2.0 = 35 years versus 70 / 3.5 = 20 years.
Remember that each year's percentage gain compounds on top of all prior gains.

options_template.text: Because annual gains compound exponentially: Country X doubles twice (4x, to ~$80k) while Country Y doubles 3.5 times (~11x, to ~$222k), leaving Country Y nearly 2.8 times richer per person.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Compounding magnifies small annual growth gaps over decades, turning a 1.5-percentage-point annual edge into nearly triple the living standard within 70 years.

options_template.text: Because Country Y's living standard will be only 1.5% higher than Country X's in 2096, making the policy reform largely irrelevant.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Single-Year Difference Error): A 1.5-percentage-point difference applies *every single year* and compounds over 70 years—it is not a one-time 1.5% gap.

options_template.text: Because Country Y's living standard will be exactly 105% higher (70 * 1.5%) in 2096 due to linear accumulation.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Linear Accumulation Fallacy): Multiplying 70 * 1.5% ignores compounding; exact compound growth leaves Country Y roughly 178% higher (nearly 2.8x Country X's income).

options_template.text: Because Country X's real GDP per capita will actually shrink below $20,000 whenever its growth rate is below 3.0%.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Positive Growth Misinterpretation): Growing at +2.0% per year still quadruples Country X's income over 70 years; it simply lags far behind Country Y.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Total GDP vs. GDP per Capita Critique
questions.title: Evaluating Aggregate GDP Growth Amid Rapid Population Expansion
questions.prompt_template: A government minister celebrates that aggregate real GDP grew by 3.0% per year over the past decade, claiming that average citizens are steadily becoming wealthier. However, census data reveal that the country's population and labor force also grew by 3.0% per year over the same decade. What is the accurate economic assessment?

hints.text: Compare aggregate real GDP growth (3.0%) with population growth (3.0%) to determine real GDP per capita growth.
Recall the Clear It Up pitfall contrasting Total GDP with GDP per capita (Y/L).

options_template.text: Average living standards doubled every 23.3 years because 70 / 3.0 = 23.3.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Aggregate-to-Per-Capita Conflation): Aggregate real GDP doubles in ~23.3 years, but because population also doubles in ~23.3 years, income per person stays flat.

options_template.text: Average living standards (real GDP per capita) remained essentially stagnant because output expansion merely kept pace with population growth, leaving Y/L unchanged.
