options_template.feedback: Correct. When aggregate real GDP and population grow at the same 3.0% rate, real output per person (Y/L) grows at 0% and average material living standards do not rise.

options_template.text: Average living standards rose by 6.0% per year because output growth and population growth add together.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Additive Ratio Error): To find per-capita growth, population growth is subtracted from (not added to) aggregate real GDP growth.

options_template.text: The country achieved rapid capital deepening because a larger workforce automatically raises K/L.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Capital Dilution Reversal): Faster workforce growth dilutes K/L unless the capital stock grows even faster than the labor force.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Distinguishing a Post-Recession Rebound from a Secular Productivity Boom
questions.prompt_template: After a severe downturn leaves an economy with a -4.0% recessionary output gap, factories restart and actual real GDP surges by +4.17% in a single year to reach full employment. Why would it be a forecasting mistake to project that the economy can now grow at +4.17% every year for the next decade?

hints.text: Compare Stage 1 (cyclical rebound from R to E_1) with Stage 2 (long-run secular growth of Potential GDP Y*).
Once idle workers are already rehired, can the economy keep rehiring them again next year?

options_template.text: Because once full employment is reached, real GDP must immediately fall by 4.17% the following year.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Mandatory Crash Myth): Reaching full employment does not force a recession; growth simply moderates to the underlying secular pace of Potential GDP.

options_template.text: Because the Rule of 70 forbids any economy from growing faster than 2.0% per year.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Rule of 70 Misinterpretation): The Rule of 70 is an approximation tool for doubling time, not a physical cap on growth rates.

options_template.text: Because the +4.17% surge was a one-time cyclical rebound closing an interior output gap (R -> E_1); once full capacity is restored, ongoing growth is limited by the slower secular expansion of Potential GDP (Y*).
options_template.feedback: Correct. You can only rehire unemployed workers and restart idle factories once; after reaching PPF_1, sustained growth depends on capital deepening and TFP growth shifting Y* outward.

options_template.text: Because restarting shuttered factories permanently eliminates Total Factor Productivity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (TFP Misconception): Reopening idle plants restores utilization without harming Total Factor Productivity.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Level Effects vs. Permanent Growth Effects in the Solow Model
questions.prompt_template: In the Solow Neoclassical Growth Model, a government enacts tax incentives that permanently raise the national saving rate (s) from 20% to 28%, while Total Factor Productivity (A) remains constant. What is the long-run macroeconomic outcome?

hints.text: Distinguish a permanent increase in the *level* of income (y*) from a permanent increase in the *growth rate* of income.
Remember what happens once the economy reaches its new steady state k*.

options_template.text: Real GDP per worker grows faster forever, permanently doubling the economy's long-run annual growth rate.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Permanent Growth Effect Fallacy): Because of diminishing marginal returns to capital, a higher saving rate raises growth only temporarily during the transition to the new steady state.

options_template.text: Steady-state capital per worker (k*) and output per worker (y*) both decline because higher saving permanently reduces aggregate demand.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Short-Run Demand Conflation): In the long-run Solow model, higher saving finances higher capital investment per worker, raising both k* and y*.

options_template.text: Neither the level nor the growth rate of output per worker changes at any point.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Effect Fallacy): Raising s shifts the investment curve s * A * k^alpha upward, producing transition growth and a permanently higher steady-state level y*.

options_template.text: The economy experiences faster transition growth and reaches a permanently higher steady-state level of capital (k*) and income (y*), after which sustained per-capita growth requires continuous TFP (A) progress.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A higher saving rate delivers a permanent *level* gain in k* and y*, but once the new steady state is reached, ongoing growth in y* depends on technological progress (A).

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Critiquing an Extreme Zero-Consumption Industrialization Proposal
questions.prompt_template: A central planner proposes forcing household consumption as close to zero as possible (C -> 0) so that nearly 100% of national output goes into heavy industrial machinery, claiming this will maximize long-run prosperity. Which macroeconomic critique exposes both the immediate and long-run flaws of this proposal?

hints.text: Combine the Zero-Consumption Trap (Section 2.1) with Diminishing Marginal Returns to Capital (Section 2.3).
Ask what happens to workers' ability to operate machines and to the incremental payoff of extra machines without TFP.

options_template.text: Workers require minimum consumer goods (food, housing, healthcare) to survive and operate machinery (the Zero-Consumption Trap), and pushing machinery per worker to extremes without TFP runs into severe diminishing marginal returns.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Starving consumption undermines the human workforce needed to run capital, while piling up physical machinery without innovation yields dwindling incremental output.

options_template.text: The proposal is mathematically optimal because every extra unit of capital goods yields increasing marginal returns forever.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Increasing Returns & Zero-Consumption Fallacy): Capital obeys diminishing marginal returns holding technology fixed, and workers cannot survive at C = 0.

options_template.text: The proposal fails solely because capital goods depreciate at 100% per year whereas consumer goods never wear out.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Depreciation Reversal): Consumer goods are used up immediately, while capital goods are durable assets with fractional annual depreciation rates.

options_template.text: The proposal would immediately cause hyper-rapid Total Factor Productivity growth by eliminating all household services.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (TFP Conflation): Eliminating household consumption does not create scientific innovation, software, or organizational efficiency.
